entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen25221" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen25222" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25223" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25223" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen25222" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen25224" type="x-p"/> The vanity of human courses in the works of pleasure, planting, building, equipage, amassing wealth, etc., <reference osisRef="Ecc.2.1-Ecc.2.11">Ecc 2:1-11</reference>. There is much sorrow in the labor of man, <reference osisRef="Ecc.2.22">Ecc 2:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ecc.2.23">Ecc 2:23</reference>. We should enjoy what the providence of God gives, <reference osisRef="Ecc.2.25">Ecc 2:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ecc.2.26">Ecc 2:26</reference>. <div eID="gen25224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25225" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen25225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25226" type="x-p"/> I will prove thee with mirth - This is well expressed by the author so often referred to. Wisdom preferable to folly, Ecc 2:12-14 ; yet little difference between the wise and the foolish in the events of life, Ecc 2:15-17 . The vanity of amassing wealth for heirs, when whether they will be foolish or wise cannot be ascertained, Ecc 2:18-21 . There is much sorrow in the labor of man, Ecc 2:22 , Ecc 2:23 . We should enjoy what the providence of God gives, Ecc 2:25 , Ecc 2:26 . Verse 1 I will prove thee with mirth - This is well expressed by the author so often referred to. Having tried speculative knowledge in vain, passion and appetite whisper: - "From the rugged thorny road Of wisdom, which so ill repays thy toil, Turn back, and enter pleasure's flowery paths. Go, take thy fill of joy, to passion give The reins; nor let one serious thought restrain What youth and affluence prompt."

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen25231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25232" type="x-p"/> I said of laughter, It is mad - Literally "To laughter I said, O mad one! and to mirth, What is this one doing?" <div eID="gen25232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25233" type="x-p"/> Solomon does not speak here of a sober enjoyment of the things of this world, but of intemperate pleasure, whose two attendants, laughter and mirth are introduced by a beautiful prosopopoeia as two persons; and the contemptuous manner wherewith he treats them has something remarkably striking. He tells the former to her face that she is mad; but as to the latter, he thinks her so much beneath his notice, that he only points at her, and instantly turns his back.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen25233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25234" type="x-p"/> To give myself unto wine, (yet acquainting [נהג noheg, "guiding"] mine heart with wisdom) - I did not run into extremes, as when I gave up myself to mirth and pleasure. There, I threw off all restraint; here, I took the middle course, to see whether a moderate enjoyment of the things of the world might not produce that happiness which I supposed man was created to enjoy here below.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen25235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25236" type="x-p"/> I made one gardens and orchards - פרדסים pardesim, "paradises." I doubt much whether this be an original Hebrew word. ferdoos, is found in the Persian and Arabic; and signifies a pleasant garden, a vineyard. Hence our word paradise, a place full of delights. How well Solomon was qualified to form gardens, orchards, vineyards, conservatories, etc., may be at once conceived when we recollect his knowledge of natural history; and that he wrote treatises on vegetables and their properties, from the cedar to the hyssop.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen25238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25239" type="x-p"/> Servants and maidens - For my works, fields, folds, and various domestic labors. <div eID="gen25239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25240" type="x-p"/> Servants born in any house - Besides those hired from without, he had married couples in the precincts of his grounds, palaces, etc., who, when their children grew up, got them employment with themselves. <div eID="gen25240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25241" type="x-p"/> Great and small cattle - Oxen, neat, horses, asses, mules, camels, and such like; with sheep and goats. And multitudes of most of these he needed, when we are told that his household consumed daily ten stall-fed oxen, with twenty from the pasture, with a hundred sheep; besides harts, roebucks, fallow deer, fatted fowls, and other kinds of provision, Probably, such another court for splendor and expense was not in the universe.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen25241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25242" type="x-p"/> The peculiar treasure of kings and of the provinces - <div eID="gen25242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25243" type="x-p"/> 1. The tares levied off his subjects. <div eID="gen25243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25244" type="x-p"/> 2. The tribute given by the neighboring potentates. Both these make the "peculiar treasure of kings;" taxes and tribute. <div eID="gen25244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25245" type="x-p"/> Men singers and women singers - This includes all instrumental and vocal performers. These may be called the delights of the sons of men. <div eID="gen25245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25246" type="x-p"/> Musical instruments, and that of all sorts - For these seven words, there are only two in the original, שדה ושדות shiddah veshiddoth. These words are acknowledged on all hands to be utterly unknown, if not utterly inexplicable. Some render them male and female captives; others, cups and flagons; others, cooks and confectioners; others, a species of musical compositions derived from a celebrated Phoenician woman named Sido, to whom Sanchoniatha attributes the invention of music. Others, with more probability, wives and concubines; of the former of whom Solomon had seven hundred, and of the latter, three hundred; and if these be not spoken of here, they are not mentioned at all; whereas music, and every thing connected with that, was referred to before. The author of Choheleth paraphrases thus: - "To complete <div eID="gen25246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25247" type="x-p"/> This scene of earthly bliss, how large a span <div eID="gen25247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25248" type="x-p"/> Of that which most delights the sons of men <div eID="gen25248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25249" type="x-p"/> Fell to my portion! What a lovely train <div eID="gen25249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25250" type="x-p"/> Of blooming beauties, by connubial ties, <div eID="gen25250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25251" type="x-p"/> By purchase, or the gifts of neighboring kings, <div eID="gen25251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25252" type="x-p"/> Or spoils of war, made mine." <div eID="gen25252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25253" type="x-p"/> If, after all this, I may add one conjecture, it shall be this; שדה sadeh, in Hebrews is a field, and occurs in various parts of the Bible. שדות sadoth is fields, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.7">1Sam 22:7</reference>, the points in such a case are of no consideration. May not Solomon be speaking here of farms upon farms, or estates upon estates, which he had added by purchase to the common regal portion? We know that a king of Israel (Ahab) once desired to have a vineyard (Naboth's) which he could not obtain: now, Solomon having spoken before of gardens, orchards, and vineyards, why may he not here speak of supernumerary estates? Perhaps every man who critically examines the place will be dissatisfied, and have a conjecture of his own.

entries.content_plain: Verse 14 The wise man's eyes, etc. - Well expressed by Choheleth: - "The wise are circumspect, maturely weigh The consequence of what they undertake, Good ends propose, and fittest means apply To accomplish their designs." But the fool walketh in darkness - "But fools, deprived Of reason's guidance, or in darkness grope, Or, unreflecting like a frantic man, Who on the brink of some steep precipice Attempts to run a race with heedless steps, Rush to their own perdition." One event happeneth to them all - "Though wide the difference, what has human pride To boast? Even I myself too plainly saw, That one event to both alike befalls; To various accidents of life exposed, Without distinction: nor can wisdom screen From dangers, disappointments, grief, and pain."

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen25274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25275" type="x-p"/> As it happeneth to the fool - Literally, "According as the event is to the fool, it happens to me, even me." There is a peculiar beauty and emphasis in the repetition of me. Having pointed out the advantages that wisdom has over folly, he takes this opportunity of reminding us of the danger of trusting too much to it, by showing that it is equally subject to the common accidents of life; and, therefore, incapable of making us completely happy. Having given his sentiments on this point in general terms, he proceeds to those particular instances wherein human prudence chiefly exerts itself; and shows how egregiously it is mistaken in every one of them - C.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen25283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25284" type="x-p"/> For there is a man - Does he not allude to himself?
